1. Introduction
This Facilitator Guide has been developed to support the effective implementation of the Sudan
Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns (MSSN) – 2026.
It provides practical, step-by-step guidance to facilitators on:
● Planning and organizing the training
● Delivering high-quality, competency-based sessions
● Facilitating skills practice and clinical learning
● Assessing participant competence
● Adapting training to real hospital constraints in Sudan
This guide is intended to be used together with:
● The Sudan Training Manual for Management of Sick and Small Newborn – 2026
● Participant modules and job aids
● Skills checklists and assessment tools
1.1 National Context and Alignment
Care of sick and small newborns is a strategic priority under the Sudan Newborn Action Plan (2022–
Neonatal mortality remains a major public health challenge in Sudan. Most preventable neonatal
deaths are due to:
● Birth asphyxia
● Prematurity and its complications
● Neonatal sepsis
● Delayed recognition and referral of sick newborns
This training course and facilitator guide are designed to:
● Strengthen hospital-based newborn care
● Improve early recognition and timely management
● Standardize care across facilities
● Build practical clinical competence among doctors, nurses, and midwives

t: ● What are the major causes of newborn death?
o Asphyxia, sepsis and prematurity.
● What are underlying causes of death?
o Not breathing, hypothermia, not breastfeeding.
● Why is hypothermia dangerous to newborns?
o Hypothermia can cause newborns to have infection, coagulation defects, acidosis,
delayed fetal-to-newborn circulatory adjustment, hyaline membrane disease
(respiratory distress syndrome) and brain haemorrhage. It is dangerous.
● What are major causes of hypothermia?
o Cold room with draft (convection), being wet (evaporation), touching cold surfaces
(conduction), being exposed (radiation).
● What actions can health workers perform to prevent hypothermia?
o Ensure room temperature of 25–28 °C. Close all windows, turn off fan and air-
conditioning to ensure there is no draught (i.e. airflow) in the room. Dry baby
thoroughly and then cover; put in skin-to-skin contact with the mother. For the rare
resuscitation that would be needed, turn on the radiant warmer (if available) before
delivery or cover the resuscitation area surface with a clot
● Can we predict which babies will not be breathing?
o Even babies born of mothers with no risk factors may not breathe.
22 | Page
FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
● Is it important to prepare the newborn resuscitation area?
o Even though rare, we cannot predict which babies will not breathe at birth. Thus, we
need the newborn resuscitation area set up for all deliveries.
● How do we prepare the delivery space?
o Ensure that all delivery equipment and supplies are available, clean, and ready for
use. Lay out in sequence: gloves*, gauze, povidone-iodine, 2 cloths, oxytocin, needle
and syringe, 2 cord clamps** and sterile scissors.
o Aside from cloth, ventilation bag and mask, ensure that suction device, hat and
clock/timer are in easy reach/view of the newborn resuscitation area. All equipment
should be tested before the delivery.
o If only one provider handles the mother’s and the newborn’s cord sections, 2 pairs of
gloves should be worn. The outer pair should be removed prior to handling the cord.
● Why is drying important?
o It stimulates breathing. Most babies who are not breathing at birth will start to breathe
after thorough drying.
o It prevents hypothermia.
● How do we dry well?
o Before delivery, place a clean cloth over the mother’s bare abdomen. Deliver the baby
and place on the clean cloth. Drying should be immediate (within a few seconds of
delivery), thorough and systematic. Wipe the eyes, mouth/nose, face, head, front,
back, arms and legs. Thorough drying takes around 30 seconds. It should be by
rubbing, not patting, but should not remove the vernix. Assess the baby for breathing
during drying.
● Why is skin-to-skin contact good?
o It keeps a baby warm, promotes bonding, contributes to overall success of
breastfeeding/ colostrum feeding, stimulates the immune system (mucosa-associated
lymphoid tissue), protects from hypoglycaemia, and helps colonization with maternal
skin flora (friendly family bacteria).
● How do we maintain direct skin-to-skin contact?
o You have just finished drying the baby. Remove the wet cloth so that the baby is in
direct skin-to-skin contact with the mother’s bare abdomen. Cover, but do not wrap,
23 | Page
FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
the baby with another clean dry cloth. This keeps the skin of the baby’s abdomen
directly in contact with the skin of the mother’s abdomen. Cover the newborn’s head
with a hat.
● Why should we delay cord clamping until after the cord stops pulsating?
o Delaying cord-clamping protects against anaemia, intraventricular haemorrhage and
necrotizing enterocolitis.
● How do we know the cord is pulsating?
o Demonstrate with the manikin. Ask every participant to look and to feel the cord.
● Why should we stop our usual practice of clamping the cord far from the umbilical base for later
trimming?
o Unnecessary handling of the cord gives opportunity for bacteria to get into the cord.
o Cutting at 2 cm (between the clamps/ties) eliminates the need to “trim” the cord later.
● Should we apply disinfectant to the cord?
o No. If allowed to air dry, the cord will dry more quickly. Remind participants that
they need to tell caretakers: “Do not use a binder or apply any substance to the cord.”
● Why should we call out the time of delivery precise to the second?
o Actions in the first minute especially need timing to the second. Thorough drying
takes around 30 seconds. A baby not breathing after 30 seconds needs to be helped to
breathe/ or have lungs aerated within 60 seconds. The cord should be clamped after
cord stops pulsating at 1–3 minutes.
● Why is unnecessary handling bad?
● Each time a health worker handles a baby, the baby is at risk for infection and cold.
● When should a health worker handle the baby?
o Only when there is a medical need.
● When should a health worker perform hand hygiene (handwashing or alcohol hand rub)?
o Immediately before and immediately after handling a baby/mother or their
surroundings, after exposure to body fluids, and before and after an aseptic procedure.
● When should a baby be suctioned?
o Only when the airway is blocked and baby is completely not breathing, for example, a
non-vigorous, meconium-stained baby.

● Does a baby with thick meconium staining but who is breathing well need suctioning?
o No. The baby is breathing well and suctioning does not prevent meconium aspiration.
● Why is suctioning a baby dangerous? (Ask for as many answers as possible.)
o Hold the bulb up. Pretend to suction a participant, then move to the next and ask if it
is OK to suction them with this. Ask why. Do the same for five participants. Bulbs are
dirty even when cleaning has been attempted. You cannot get rid of all the bacteria.
Suction bulbs spread infection. Ask if they would feel comfortable if you suctioned
them. Ask why. Gagging a baby is dangerous. It can cause the baby to stop breathing
and get sick. It can cause trauma to the mouth and nose.

Step 1: Simulator Preparation
● Fill both bags of the MamaBreast simulator with exactly 500 ml of water each, strictly
avoiding the use of real milk to prevent damage to the equipment.
● Assist the volunteer in putting on the MamaBreast simulator.
● Adjust the waist strap to ensure a secure, comfortable fit around the side, and adjust the neck
strap so the breasts sit at a natural height.
Step 2: Demonstrating Good Positioning
● Hand the newborn doll to the volunteer and instruct them to hold the baby close to their body.
● Demonstrate that the neonate's head and body must be aligned in a straight line, ensuring the
neck is neither twisted nor bent.
● Show participants how to support the baby's entire body rather than just the head and neck,
which is particularly vital when handling neonates under 28 days old.
● Position the baby so they are facing the breast, with their nose directly opposite the nipple, to
encourage the rooting reflex.
Step 3: Demonstrating Good Attachment
● Verbally outline the four key clinical signs of a proper latch while the volunteer acts out the
motion with the doll.
● Chin: The baby's chin should firmly touch the breast.
● Mouth: The baby's mouth must be open wide.
● Lip: The baby's lower lip should be curled or turned outward.
● Areola: More of the mother's areola should be visible above the baby's upper lip than below
the lower lip.
Instruct the volunteer to bring the baby to the breast (not the breast to the baby) to simulate achieving
this attachment on the MamaBreast

t: Why is breastfeeding beneficial?
● Breastfeeding is one of the most life-saving interventions we have. Delays in initiation of
breastfeeding are associated with dramatic increase in death and illness. Babies who are fed
formula have 4–6 times the risk of dying compared with exclusively breastfed babies.
Formula is more dangerous to a newborn than is smoking to an adult.
When is a typical baby ready to breastfeed?
● Never immediately after birth. Leave the baby between the mother’s breasts in continuous
skin-to-skin contact. The baby may want to rest for 20–30 minutes or even longer before
showing signs of readiness to breastfeed (i.e. feeding cues). Just under half of all babies
initiate breastfeeding naturally after one hour from birth.
● Note: Please explain to the participants that babies should not be forced onto the breast or
have the nipple forced into the mouth. Wait for the feeding cues.
What are the feeding cues that a baby is ready to breastfeed?
● The earliest sign is drooling, followed by mouth opening, tonguing, licking, rooting and
biting of fingers or hand. Eventually, the baby will locate the breast and open his/her mouth
widely to attach to the breast.
Do some mothers not have enough milk?
● Studies in very poor countries (Ecuador, Nigeria) showed that all mothers (many of whom
were severely malnourished) were able physiologically to breastfeed. A newborn’s stomach

is only the size of your thumbnail. It may not be perceived that the baby has gotten enough
milk.
● If the baby appears to be fussy or dissatisfied at the mother’s breast, first ensure that no other
liquids are being given, i.e. formula, sugar water or other fluids.
● Counsel the mother on offering her breasts 8–12 times over the day and night upon her
baby’s early feeding cues.
● Stimulation of the breast by the baby’s sucking results in messages being sent to the mother’s
brain and back to the breast to produce more milk. Thus, milk production will increase if the
mother’s breast is stimulated more frequently through offering the breast more often.
What are signs of good feeding position?
● The baby’s head and body are in a straight line (neck is not twisted or flexed), the baby is
facing the breast, with nose opposite nipple, the mother is holding the baby’s body close to
her body and supporting the baby’s whole body (not just neck and shoulders).
● What are signs of good attachment?
● More areola is visible above the baby’s mouth than below; the mouth is wide open with the
lower lip turned outward, the baby’s chin touching breast; sucking is slow and deep with
occasional pauses.
● Note: Signs of ineffective attachment include in-drawing of newborn’s cheeks, lip-smacking
sounds or mother’s nipple pain
How can we improve attachment?
● By touching the baby’s lips with her nipple, waiting until the mouth is opened wide, moving
baby quickly onto breast, aiming baby’s lower lip well below nipple; also, by trying different
positions, e.g. sitting upright or laying on her side

rows: Demonstration: Synchronized Positive pressure ventilation with Chest Compression
Two facilitators are needed — one gives ventilation, one gives compressions. This shows
participants from the very start that this is teamwork, and not a one-person job.
“So far you have practised ventilation. Now we come to the baby who does not improve. This is
the baby whose heart rate stays below 60 even after we have given good ventilation. Watch us
carefully — then each of you will do it yourselves.”

t: Step 1 — Say when to start
“We do not start compressions early. We start only when the heart rate is still less than 60 after at
least 30 seconds of PPV that is moving the chest. If the chest is not moving, the answer is better
ventilation — not compressions.”
Step 2 — Show the position
• Move to the head of the bed to give compressions; the ventilator stays at the side.
• This leaves space for safe insertion of an umbilical venous catheter.
• Baby on a firm flat surface, back supported, neck slightly extended.
Step 3 — Show the landmark
• Thumbs on the lower third of the sternum, just below the imaginary line joining the two nipples.
• Encircle the chest with both hands, fingers supporting the back.
• Show the two-thumb method — state clearly that this is the preferred method.
Step 4 — Show the depth
• Press down about one-third of the antero-posterior diameter of the chest.
37 | Page
FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
• Allow the chest to come back up fully between compressions, but keep the thumbs resting on
the skin.
Step 5 — Show the oxygen
• Increase oxygen to 100% once compressions begin.
• Check the pulse oximeter signal.
Step 6 — Show the rhythm (the key skill)
Demonstrate slowly first, then at speed. Everyone says it out loud together:
“One – and – Two – and – Three – and – Breathe – and…”
• Compressor says: One, Two, Three
• Ventilator squeezes on: Breathe
• 3 compressions : 1 breath = one cycle
• 15 cycles in 30 seconds
• Per minute: 90 compressions + 30 breaths = 120 events
Let the whole class chant the rhythm twice before anyone touches a manikin.
Step 7 — Show the check
After 60 seconds of coordinated compressions and ventilation, pause and check the heart rate. A
cardiac monitor is preferred; auscultation is acceptable — count the beats in 6 seconds and multiply
by 10.
• HR ≥ 60 → stop chest compressions, continue PPV at 40–60 breaths/min.
• HR still < 60 → continue compressions and PPV, give epinephrine, and obtain emergency
vascular access (umbilical venous catheter).
Step 8 — Common mistakes to name out loud
• Starting compressions when the chest was never moving.
• Compressing and squeezing the bag at the same time.
• Going too fast and losing the 3:1 ratio.
• Lifting the thumbs off the chest between compressions.
• Stopping to check the heart rate before 60 seconds.

3.3 Oropharyngeal Airway
The oropharyngeal airway is not the first answer to a baby who is not breathing. The first answer is
always position, clear the airway, and good bag-and-mask ventilation. The airway is used when the
tongue or the pharynx is blocking, and reposition has not worked.

rows: “You have a baby, you have positioned the head, you have cleared the mouth, and you are
squeezing the bag — but the chest is still not moving. One of the reasons is the tongue falling
back. This small piece of plastic can solve it in seconds. Watch.”

t: Step 1 — When to use it
• When bag-and-mask ventilation stays ineffective because of airway obstruction, after reposition
and suction have already been tried.
• In a baby with Pierre Robin sequence (small chin, tongue falling back) — here it may be needed
early.
• In choanal atresia, where the nose is blocked and the baby cannot breathe through the mouth.
• In a floppy baby whose tongue and soft tissues collapse the pharynx.
Step 2 — When NOT to use it
• In a baby with an active gag reflex — it may cause vomiting, laryngospasm or bradycardia.
• As a substitute for repositioning the head. Try the correct position first.
• It does not protect the airway from aspiration.
Step 3 — Choose the size
How to measure: hold the airway along the side of the baby’s face. The flange should be at the level
of the lips, and the tip should reach the angle of the jaw.
45 | Page
FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
• Too small — it will push the tongue back and make the obstruction worse.
• Too large — it will press on the epiglottis and obstruct the larynx, or cause bradycardia.
Step 4 — Insert it (the newborn way)
1. Position the baby: neck slightly extended, on a firm flat surface.
2. Open the mouth with the finger and thumb.
3. Depress the tongue with a tongue depressor or the blade of a laryngoscope.
4. Insert the airway with the curve following the natural curve of the tongue — concave side
down, the same way it will sit.
5. Slide it gently over the tongue until the flange rests on the lips.
Do NOT insert it upside down and rotate 180° as is done in adults. The newborn palate is soft and
this will damage it.
6. Reapply the mask and give PPV. Look at the chest.
7. If the chest now moves — the obstruction was the tongue. Continue ventilation.
8. If the chest still does not move — recheck the seal, the position, and the secretions; then think
about an alternative airway (laryngeal mask or ET tube).
Step 5 — After insertion
• Watch continuously — the airway can be pushed out or blocked by secretions.
• Suction only if secretions are visible and are impairing ventilation.
• Monitor SpO₂ and heart rate.
• Remove it as soon as the baby is breathing well or a definitive airway is placed.
Step 6 — Common mistakes to name out loud
• Reaching for the airway before trying to reposition the head.
• Guessing the size instead of measuring against the face.
• Rotating it 180° like in an adult.
• Forcing it against resistance.
• Inserting it in a baby who is gagging.

3.4 Intubation
Prerequisites
• Pre-oxygenate before intubation — PPV with 100% oxygen.
• Deliver free-flow oxygen during intubation.
• Not more than 20 seconds per attempt; not more than 3 attempts.
• Ventilate with bag and mask with 100% oxygen in between attempts.
Preparation
1. Assessment: assess the need for intubation based on the newborn’s clinical condition and
response to initial resuscitation measures.
2. Gather equipment: ensure all necessary equipment for intubation, including a laryngoscope,
endotracheal tube, suction, and securing devices, is readily available and prepared.
3. The intubation set for emergency intubation in the delivery room should always be ready and
checked before receiving the baby.
4. For equipment preparation, see the setup equipment in the mechanical ventilation section.
Equipment
• Bag and mask (sizes 0, 1)
• Oxygen cylinder
• Suction machine (pressure set at 80–100 mmHg) with suction catheters
• Sterile water, sterile gloves
• Laryngoscope with blades (size 00, 0, 1) with extra bulb
• Pulse oximeter, scissors, tape, stethoscope
• Stylet and end-tidal CO₂ detector

8. Bring the posterior larynx and vocal cords into view.
9. Hold the tube high up and with the natural slope facing forward, as it is easier to direct.
10. Feed the tube in from the side to allow visualisation of it passing through the cords.

12. Adjust to the previously measured naso-tragal + 1 cm measurement.
13. Be cautious as to how far to insert the tube, as it is often too far in.
14. Secure the ETT against the roof of the palate or firmly at the lips.
15. Carefully remove the laryngoscope and introducer (if used).
16. Confirm ETT position: chest rise, auscultate for air entry, and connect the CO₂ detector and
ventilation circuit to confirm correct ETT position.
17. Secure the ETT with an appropriate fixation device, ensuring a good seal to the skin and
avoiding traction on the ETT.

Signs the ET Tube is in the Oesophagus
• Poor response to intubation (cyanosis, bradycardia, etc.)
• CO₂ detector fails to show presence of expired CO₂
• No audible breath sounds
• Air heard entering the stomach
• Gastric distension may be seen
• No mist in the tube
• Poor chest movements
Signs the ET Tube is Too Far in the Trachea
• Heart rate or colour shows no improvement
• Breath sounds heard over the right and not on the left side of the chest
• Breath sounds are louder on the right side of the chest than on the left
Post-Intubation Care
Continuously monitor the newborn’s vital signs, oxygenation and ventilation after successful
intubation.
1. Chest X-ray is the gold standard in confirming the correct ETT position; the ET tip should be
visible 1 cm above the carina (T2–T3).
2. Consider shortening the ETT to minimise dead space.
3. Ensure blades are sent for sterilisation as per unit protocol.
4. Ensure accurate documentation of the procedure, including the position of the ETT on chest X-
ray and whether or not adjustments were made.
Update the parents.

t: ● What do you do when the baby starts breathing well?
■ Return the baby to the mother in skin-to-skin contact.
■ Explain to the mother that the baby had difficulty breathing but is doing better now
■ Mother should let the health worker know if the baby has problems with breathing again.
■ Counsel her on the baby’s feeding cues, etc.
■ Monitor the baby every 15 minutes for breath-ing and warmth.
● If baby is not breathing, what do you do?
■ Check heart rate after one minute of bag-and-mask ventilation.
● How do we quickly check heart rate?
■ First, without pausing the ventilation, look at the cord. If there are no visible cord pulsations,
either put fingers on umbilical stump near abdomen, or use a stethoscope:
■ Count the number of beats in six seconds, then multiply by 10 to get the beats per minute.
This is accurate enough to indicate if the heart rate is < 100 or > 100 beats per minute (bpm).
● If heart rate is < 100 bpm, what do you do?
■ If heart rate is between 60 and 100 bpm, do ventilation corrective steps, then resume
ventilation and check heart rate again at 3 minutes; continue effective ventilation if heart rate
is < 100 bpm.
■ If heart rate is < 60 bpm, do ventilation corrective steps, resume ventilation.
● If heart rate is > 100 bpm and the baby is not breathing well, what do you do?
■ (Ventilate more slowly.)
58 | Page
FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
● Why?
■ We ventilated too quickly and did not give the baby a chance to breathe.
● If after 10 minutes of ventilation the baby has a heart rate but is still not breathing (or is having
difficulty breathing; has severe chest in-drawing, for example), what do we do?
■ Continue bag-and-mask ventilation, refer, ensure warm transport, and accompany the baby,
preferably with the mother, to hospital.
● If after 10 minutes of effective ventilation, the baby has no heart rate and is not breathing, what
do you do?
■ The baby is dead. Stop ventilation, provide emotional support to the mother, and record the
event.
● If after 20 minutes of effective ventilation, the baby is still not breathing and the heart rate is < 60
bpm, what do you do?
■ Stop ventilation. Explain to the mother that the baby still has not started to breathe and the
baby’s weak heart beat was not enough to give oxygen to the brain. Babies’ hearts that are as
weak as your baby’s usually stop beating soon.
● How many babies will need bag-and-mask ventilation?
■ If we dry babies well, only a few out of a hundred newborns.
● How do we position the mask?
■ Ask participants to demonstrate by: placing the mask over the baby’s chin, mouth and nose;
do not cover the eyes with the mask. Form a firm seal between the mask and the face (use
mask size 1 for normal-birth-weight newborn and size 0 for low-birth-weight newborn).
Squeeze the bag a few times to observe the rise of the chest.
● How do we know if the ventilation is adequate?
■ Chest is rising, baby’s heart rate rises, and baby gradually becomes pink.
● What do we do if the chest is not rising sufficiently?
■ Reposition head so neither flexed nor hyperextended, and lift chin. Should these fail,
reposition mask to get a better seal, check airway for blockage, squeeze bag harder. The bag
and mask should have been checked prior to resuscitation.
● How often should we squeeze the bag?
■ 40 times per minute (30–50 acceptable).
59 | Page
FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
● What should we do when the baby starts breathing?
■ Stop ventilation and observe to ensure that the baby continues to breathe well. Assess
breathing. If breathing 30–60 breaths per minute without severe chest in-drawing, put the
baby in direct skin-to-skin contact on the mother’s chest and do routine newborn care
including observation for feeding cues. Reassure the mother, monitor every 15 minutes.
● How often should we reassess baby’s breathing and heart rate?
■ Every 1–2 minutes.
● Why would a baby have a good heart rate but not breathe?
Bag-and-mask ventilation may be too fast. We need to slow down the number of squeezes per
minute to allow the baby the chance to breathe on her own

Question 1: What is your primary assessment?
Answer: Neonatal shock (cold type), complicated by respiratory distress and hypoglycaemia.
Question 2: What is your immediate and targeted management using the ABC approach?
Airway (A) & Breathing (B):
• Secure the airway.
• Administer oxygen to treat the hypoxaemia and respiratory distress.
Circulation (C):
• Establish IV access immediately and draw labs (blood culture, metabolic panel).
• Fluids: give normal saline or Ringer’s lactate.
– Calculation: 20 ml/kg × 3 kg = 60 ml. Give over 15 to 30 minutes. (Reduce to 10 ml/kg =
30 ml if cardiogenic shock is suspected.)
• Antibiotics: give broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics immediately after drawing the cultures.
• Support: prepare vasopressors (epinephrine or dopamine) if hypotension persists after the 60
ml fluid bolus.
Dextrose / Disability (D):
• Treat the hypoglycaemia immediately to prevent further neurological deterioration.
• Dextrose: give 10% dextrose (D10W).
– Calculation: 2 ml/kg × 3 kg = 6 ml IV bolus.
Question 3: What indicators show the baby is improving?
• Normalized heart rate and blood pressure.
• Stronger pulses, warm extremities, improved skin perfusion.
• Improved alertness and return of normal reflexes — no longer lethargic.
Follow-up labs showing normal blood glucose, corrected metabolic acidosis, and reduced lactate.

Portable oxygen needed = 2 × [FiO₂ flow (L/min) × expected journey time (minutes)]. A full transfer
cylinder contains 250 L.

checkpoint? Take a second cylinder.”

The Eight Counselling Points
The provider should counsel the family on:
1. The reason for the need for transfer — non-availability of higher facilities in the SNCU.

7. What care or treatment is likely to be given at the tertiary level.

7. Admission of newborn
7.1 Triage of the Newborn at the SCNU
Lecture (Triaging Newborn at Entry of Neonatal unit)
What Triage Is?
Triage is a quick assessment and sorting process used to evaluate and categorize sick newborns
shortly after they arrive at the special care newborn unit. It helps prioritize care and treatment based
on the severity of the condition and the resources available.
Triage is about priority and speed. Triage should take less than 60 seconds.
“Triage is not diagnosis. You are not asking ‘what is wrong with this baby?’ You are asking one
question only: ‘can this baby wait?’ That question must be answered in less than a minute.”
The Three Groups
The provider carries out a brief, focused assessment and places the newborn in one of three groups:
1. Emergency signs (danger signs) — the newborn is critically ill and at immediate risk of death if
urgent intervention is not provided.
2. Priority signs — the baby needs prompt attention and should be moved ahead in the queue for

Why It Matters
The admission process can be challenging and involves several key steps to ensure the baby's
immediate stabilization and comprehensive care. These steps need to be well organized, smooth and
time-effective, aiming to increase Golden Hour success rates, decrease staff stress, and ultimately
improve patient outcomes.
Admission of newborns, particularly sick newborns, is a crucial part of the Golden Hour of the
baby's life. The clock does not stop at the door of your unit.

(c) Maintaining Stability and Monitoring
Once in the SCNU, the baby is closely monitored:
• Vital signs, oxygen saturation, body temperature and other physiological parameters.
• Maintenance of warmth to prevent serious hypothermia is crucial.
• Incubator temperature (servo or manual) and humidity adjustment is very vital on admission.
• Wrapping the baby with plastic bags may be needed, especially for extreme and VLBW infants.
• The degree of respiratory distress and the efficacy of respiratory support should be monitored
and adjusted as needed.
• Blood glucose monitoring and judicious management of hypoglycaemia is crucial to prevent
serious CNS complications of hypoglycaemia.
Writing and Reviewing Admission Orders
The Rule: The most senior paediatrician or neonatologist may need to give some verbal orders
during the assessment. However, the final admission orders should be written and recorded
immediately after finishing the assessment. The orders should be very clear and in a systematic
manner.
“Verbal orders are for the first five minutes only. If it is still verbal after the assessment is finished, it
is not an order — it is a rumour.”

Reviewing the Orders — The Safety Step
• The orders must be recorded and reviewed by nursing staff — at least 2 nurses.
• Any confusion or unclear order should be clarified with the medical staff immediately.
• All requested blood samples should be withdrawn as soon as possible.
• IV medications are administered as soon as the IV line is ready.
• The nursing staff prepares for all procedures and assists the medical staff during procedures
such as fixation of central lines.
Two nurses reviewing is not bureaucracy. It is the last barrier between a decimal point and a dead
baby. Apply patient and medication safety practices: correct patient ID, double-check doses, use of
order sheets.

7.3 Golden hour of life
Goals
1. To understand the concept of the Golden Hour.
2. To know the significance of Golden Hour interventions.
3. To gain an approach that uses the best available evidence, aiming to implement safe, effective
and timely interventions.
4. Prevention of hypothermia.
5. Support of respiration.
6. Support of the cardiovascular system.
7. Support of nutrition and hydration.
8. Prevention of sepsis.
What the First Hour Includes
1. Early essential newborn care and neonatal resuscitation.
2. Post-resuscitation care.
3. Transportation of the sick newborn to the neonatal intensive care unit.
4. Respiratory and cardiovascular support, and nutrition support.
5. The initial course in the SCNU.
Look at that list again. Everything you have trained on this week is in it — the golden minute,
resuscitation, compressions, intubation, vascular access, transport, triage, admission. The Golden
Hour is not a new topic. It is the thread that ties the whole course together.
Why It Matters
Neonatal management in the first hour of life has an important effect on both the immediate and the
long-term outcomes of all neonates.
The studies that evaluated the concept of the golden hour in preterm neonates showed a marked
reduction in:
1. Hypothermia
2. Hypoglycaemia
3. Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH)
4. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD)
5. Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP)

8.1 Prematurity & low birth weight complications
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, participants will be able to:
• Define prematurity and classify preterm newborns according to gestational age and birth weight.
• Describe the basic pathophysiological concepts underlying prematurity.
• Identify common complications of prematurity, associated risk factors, and their impact on
neonatal health.
• Apply evidence-based management protocols for prematurity and its major complications.
And for the admitted baby specifically, participants will be able to:
• Decide the appropriate place of care by birth weight.
• Describe the care of a LBW baby and the daily monitoring required.
• Describe Kangaroo Mother Care, and help a mother start skin-to-skin care.
• Help a mother breastfeed a LBW baby.
• Recognise danger signs and know when to escalate or refer.
Interactive Lecture: complication of prematurity
• Ask participants to raise their hands if they have cared for a LBW baby.
• Ask several who raised their hands to describe the problems they have seen.
• List these on the flip chart.

“Keep that list on the wall for the whole session. Every problem you have just named is in this
chapter. By the end of today you will have an answer for each one — and you will notice how many
of the answers are free.”
Set the Scale of the Problem
• Preterm birth complications are the leading cause of death among children under 5 years of age.
Three-quarters of these deaths could be prevented with current, cost-effective interventions.
• Across countries, the rate of preterm birth ranges from 4–16% of babies.
• Approximately 900,000 children died in 2019 of complications of preterm birth.
115 | Page
FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
• Preterm births account for approximately 70% of neonatal deaths and 36% of infant deaths, as
well as 25–50% of cases of long-term neurologic impairment in children.
In low-income settings, half of the babies born at or below 32 weeks die due to a lack of feasible,
cost-effective care such as warmth, breastfeeding support, and basic care for infections and breathing
difficulties. In high-income countries, almost all these babies survive.
Sudan: in 2023 the neonatal mortality rate was estimated at 24.8 per 1,000 live births — nearly
41,690 newborns dying annually. The stillbirth rate is estimated at 21.51 per 1,000 births, translating
into 36,973 annual deaths.

Preterm babies are defined as babies born alive before 37 weeks of pregnancy are completed.
Low birth weight (LBW) babies are those with a birth weight less than 2.5 kg, irrespective of their
period of gestation. LBW infants have a 2–3 times increased risk of mortality.

Complications are inversely proportionate to gestational age. The smaller and younger the baby, the

What KMC Is, and What It Is Not
Open With a Question
“What is Kangaroo Mother Care?”
Let them answer. Write every answer on the flip chart. Do not correct anything yet.
Most groups will say ‘skin-to-skin’ and stop there. That is exactly the gap this session closes.
The Definition — Present It as Written
Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is: care of preterm and low-birth-weight newborns in prolonged (as
close as possible to 24 hours a day, with a minimum of eight hours a day) skin-to-skin contact
initiated as soon as possible after birth, with exclusive breast milk feeding. An additional feature
where KMC is initiated in health facilities is timely discharge from the neonatal intensive or special
care unit to a lower level of care within the facility or at home, with continued skin-to-skin contact
and close monitoring.
Now go back to the flip chart and ask them to find, in their own answers, the four things the
definition contains:
1. Prolonged skin-to-skin contact — as close to 24 hours as possible, minimum 8.
2. Initiated as soon as possible after birth.
3. Exclusive breast milk feeding.
4. Timely discharge to a lower level of care, with continued skin-to-skin and close monitoring.

rows: KMC is a comprehensive care package that includes the mother-baby pair and their family,
supported by healthcare workers, aimed at minimizing separation between mother and baby
during hospitalization. It is NOT merely an intervention — it is a fundamental standard of care
for all preterm and LBW newborns.

substandard care today — the same way a baby who did not receive his antibiotics did.”

The Key Points — Teach These as the Spine of the Whole Session
• KMC is a comprehensive care package that minimizes separation between mother and baby,
involving prolonged skin-to-skin contact and exclusive breast milk feeding.
• KMC should be initiated as soon as possible after birth for all preterm and low-birth-weight
newborns, regardless of weight or gestational age.
• The goal is continuous KMC (as close to 24 hours as possible, minimum 8 hours daily) with
zero mother-baby separation.
• KMC provides immediate and long-term benefits for newborns, mothers, families and the health
system — including improved survival, neurodevelopment, breastfeeding outcomes, and
reduced hospital stay.
• KMC is safe for both stable and unstable babies, can be practised everywhere (labour room,
NICU, postnatal ward, and home), and requires no additional staff.
• Transfer of babies should ideally occur in the skin-to-skin position, and discharge criteria focus
on feeding competence and maternal readiness rather than weight alone.
• KMC is equally important for late preterm infants (34–36+6 weeks), who are often cared for in
postnatal wards and may not receive adequate skin-to-skin support.
That last point deserves a full minute. Ask: ‘who in this room has a 35-week baby on the postnatal
ward right now?’ Then ask: ‘is that baby in skin-to-skin?’ The late preterm is the baby everyone
forgets, because he looks fine.

When — As Soon As Possible After Birth
KMC should be initiated as soon as possible after birth for ALL preterm or LBW newborns. Weight
is NOT a barrier to initiation. KMC is recommended for 8–24 hours per day — as many hours as
possible.
Immediate KMC
Place the baby skin-to-skin immediately after birth, unless:
• The baby is haemodynamically unstable or unable to breathe.
• The mother is critically ill, and no substitute caregiver is available.
130 | Page

Then:
• Attempt direct feeding at the breast within the first hour.
• If unsuccessful, provide colostrum within the first hour of birth.
• Delay weighing and measuring the newborn for 60–90 minutes after birth, to allow
uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact.
Stop on that last one. Ask: ‘in your labour room, how many minutes after birth is the baby weighed?’
The answer is usually ‘immediately’. Ask why. There is no clinical reason. The scale can wait 90
minutes; the first skin-to-skin hour cannot be repeated.
Continuous KMC
• Continuation of immediate KMC — for BOTH stable and unstable babies.
• Provide skin-to-skin care for at least 18 hours per day, with ZERO separation between mother
and baby.
• For stable babies ≥ 32 weeks, continue KMC in a step-down low-care ward where mother and
baby room together with the baby in the KMC position.
• The baby should be on enteral and oral feeds — direct breastfeeding with supplementary
expressed breast milk via cup and/or gastric tube.
Intermittent KMC
• Practise intermittent KMC when immediate continuous KMC is not possible in the NICU or
newborn care unit.
• The mother or other caregiver should provide skin-to-skin sessions of at least 60–70 minutes or
longer, as many times as possible each day.
• Sessions should coincide with feeding times, with the baby in the skin-to-skin position when
receiving gastric tube feeding.

Feeding and Growth during KMC
The Feeding Order — Every Session, Every Time
Always start a feeding session by feeding DIRECTLY AT THE BREAST, then cup feeding, then
tube feeding — with the baby in the skin-to-skin position.
“Breast, then cup, then tube. In that order, every session. Not ‘he has a tube so we use the tube.’ The
tube is what finishes the feed — not what starts it. Every session begins at the breast, even if he only
manages a few sucks. That is how he learns.”

Transfer in the Skin-to-Skin Position
Transfer to a higher level of care in the skin-to-skin position whenever possible:
• From labour ward to newborn care unit or NICU.
• From NICU or newborn care unit to a lower level of care (intra-hospital or inter-hospital).
• A baby born at home should be transferred in the skin-to-skin position to a health facility.
Link this back to the transport session: the manual says the transport incubator must be prewarmed
and the baby must not leave cold. The mother IS a prewarmed transport incubator, and she never
runs out of battery.
Intra-Hospital Transfer
• Baby is secured in the skin-to-skin position; the mother may walk or be transferred in a
wheelchair, or another caregiver may carry the baby skin-to-skin.
• Mother and baby are accompanied by a healthcare worker.
• A summary of the mother's and baby's health history should be available.
Inter-Hospital Transfer
• Baby is transferred secured skin-to-skin to the mother or other caregiver, in an ambulance or an
ordinary motor vehicle.
• A healthcare worker accompanies the mother and baby.
• A summary of the mother's and baby's health history and follow-up arrangements should be
available.

Case 1 — “He Is Too Small For That”
A baby is born at 30 weeks, 1.1 kg. He is breathing with grunting, on CPAP, and has an IV line.
At 40 minutes of age the mother asks whether she can hold him. The doctor says: “not yet — he

• Is the doctor right? Quote the protocol.
• What are the ONLY two reasons to delay skin-to-skin at birth?
• What has this baby lost in the last 40 minutes?
The doctor is wrong on both counts. Weight is NOT a barrier to initiation. KMC is safe for
both stable and unstable babies. ‘When he is bigger’ is exactly backwards — the smallest, sickest
The only two exceptions: the baby is haemodynamically unstable or unable to breathe; or the
mother is critically ill and no substitute caregiver is available. He is breathing, on CPAP, with a
line. He does not meet either exception.
What he has lost: immediate KMC significantly reduces mortality, particularly within the first
72 hours. He is in the window right now, and he is spending it alone.
What should happen: skin-to-skin now, with the CPAP and the line arranged without tangles.
Attempt the breast; if not, colostrum within the first hour.

The Four Rules
1. Enteral feeds are given by gastric tube to deliver expressed breast milk to the stomach.
2. OROGASTRIC tubes are preferred in preterms with respiratory complications or on nasal
CPAP — nasogastric tubes interfere with ease of breathing.
3. All preterm babies should receive enteral feeds UPRIGHT IN THE KMC (SKIN-TO-SKIN)
POSITION, to improve absorption.
4. INTERMITTENT BOLUS feeds are preferred to continuous feeds.
Why bolus is preferred: more physiological — mimics normal feeding, promotes natural cycles of
gut hormone release (gastrin, insulin) and normal digestion; allows smaller stomach volumes at any
time, reducing reflux and associated apnoea or desaturation. Continuous feeding may be acceptable
in certain circumstances.
The Gravity Rule
The milk MUST RUN IN BY GRAVITY. Speed it up or slow it down by RAISING OR
LOWERING THE SYRINGE. IT IS DANGEROUS TO PUSH THE MILK USING THE
PLUNGER — pushing may lead to respiratory aspiration and severe complications.
“The plunger comes out and stays out. The barrel is a funnel. Your hand controls the height, and the
height controls the speed. If your thumb is on a plunger, stop — you are doing a different
procedure.”

CALCIUM: 10% calcium gluconate 1 mL/kg SLOW IV after every ~100 mL exchanged, WITH

After the Exchange
● Flush the line with saline to clear residual donor blood.
● Continue INTENSIVE PHOTOTHERAPY — rebound is common.
● Monitor vital signs, urine output, acid–base, electrolytes, calcium, glucose.
● Recheck bilirubin at 2 hours, then every 4–6 hours.
● A second exchange may be required if bilirubin rebounds.
● Treat the underlying cause — e.g. IVIG for isoimmune haemolysis.
● Document: total volume, aliquot size, duration, complications, blood details (type, donor unit,
expiry, irradiation).
● Watch for late complications: NEC, sepsis, portal vein thrombosis, infection.

rows: Case 1 — The Day-One Baby Who Looks Well
A term baby, 3.2 kg, normal delivery, is noticed to be slightly yellow at 20 hours of age. He is
feeding, active, afebrile. The midwife says: “He is only a bit yellow and he is feeding beautifully

• What does the timing tell you?
The midwife is wrong. Jaundice within the first 24 hours is NEVER physiological. ‘He looks
well’ is not reassurance — he looks well now, and bilirubin rises.
What happens next: measure TSB now and plot against age in hours. Investigate the cause —
blood group (mother and baby), Coombs, FBC and reticulocytes, G6PD. Start phototherapy per
the nomogram. Do not wait for tomorrow.

precisely because well-looking babies with early jaundice are the ones who get missed.
in the first 24 hours, the clock overrules the eye.

t: 10.1 Surveillance system
A surveillance system for neonatal sepsis is essential to monitor and prevent healthcare-associated
infections and to ensure the health and safety of newborns.
Aim: to systematically detect, report and analyze cases of neonatal sepsis in order to guide
prevention, control and quality improvement interventions, and to contribute to reduction of neonatal
morbidity and mortality.
Scope: this system surveys sepsis (blood stream infection) among preterm and sick neonates
admitted to Sudanese paediatrics and obstetrics hospitals' NICUs. It targets ALL neonates born
inside or outside hospital, whatever their clinical cause of admission. It works by identifying cases
clinically or by laboratory confirmation, collecting appropriate clinical samples (blood, CSF, swab).
The Six Objectives — Teach in This Order
1. Monitor the incidence and prevalence of neonatal sepsis.
2. Identify risk factors associated with neonatal sepsis.
3. Detect antimicrobial sensitivity and resistance patterns.
4. Evaluate the effectiveness of IPC interventions.
5. Provide data for benchmarking and quality improvement in neonatal care.
6. Facilitate timely response to outbreaks or clusters of neonatal infections.

t: The Technique
Prepare the patient
● Verify identity.
● Calm the neonate.
● Position for access — peripheral or umbilical vein.
● Clean the site with 70% alcohol — 30-SECOND SCRUB, then AIR DRY.
Confirm indication
● Suspected neonatal sepsis. No absolute contraindication; avoid sites with oedema or
infection.
Prepare materials

● Sterile gloves · 70% alcohol or chlorhexidine · sterile syringes and needles (23–25G) ·
aerobic blood culture bottles · labels · transport bag
Collect
● Use appropriate aseptic technique and follow IPC protocols — wear gloves, and DO NOT
RE-PALPATE the cleaned site.
● Collect the sample in sterile, labelled containers.
● BLOOD VOLUME: 1–2 mL per bottle — critical for detection.
● CSF VOLUME: 1 mL per bottle — critical for detection.
● If the baby is ALREADY receiving antibiotics, take the blood culture immediately BEFORE
the next dose.
Label, send, record
● Label with the neonate's name, file ID, date/time, collector's name and sample type.
● Complete the culture request form and send to the public lab using the standard transferee
procedure.
Record the sample collection in the main case record registry.

rows: “This morning you learned to find sepsis. Now the harder half: how to treat it without creating

t: The Core Regimen and Decision Pathway
● START: Ampicillin + Gentamicin for 3 days awaiting culture results.
● If NO GROWTH, repeat CRP/PCT: if negative and clinically stable, STOP ANTIBIOTICS.
● Otherwise continue: ampicillin IM/IV 50 mg/kg every 12 hours in the first week of life, and
every 8 hours after the first week, for a total of at least 10 days; PLUS gentamicin IM/IV 5
mg/kg once a day in the first week, and 7.5 mg/kg once a day after the first week, for a total
of at least 10 days.
● If CULTURE POSITIVE, continue as indicated for at least 10 days.
● Alternative: third-generation cephalosporins for a total of 2–17 days — but no or trivial
difference.
Step 2 is the whole of stewardship in one line. NO GROWTH + negative CRP/PCT + clinically
stable = STOP. Not ‘finish the course’. Not ‘just to be safe’. STOP

10.5 Antibiotic Stewardship
Antibiotic stewardship limits the development of antimicrobial-resistant organisms, and it can be
done by improving the use of antibiotics. The components:
● Use NARROW-SPECTRUM antibiotics.
● Have FIXED PROTOCOLS for starting AND stopping antibiotics.
● Start antibiotics ONLY WHEN CLINICALLY INDICATED.
● DOWNGRADE antibiotics after seeing the blood culture sensitivity pattern.
● Consider LOCAL antibiotic resistance patterns.
There is high risk of development of antibiotic resistance with the widespread use of antibiotics —
thus making careful and selective use of antibiotics to the highest-risk patients a UNIVERSAL
GOAL.

11. Essential Neonatal Procedures
Procedures and equipment are NOT taught as standalone sessions. Every procedure and every device
is taught inside the clinical session that gives the reason for using it. This document tells you where
each one lives.
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of this neonatal procedures module, participants should be able to:
● Demonstrate correct preparation and aseptic technique for neonatal procedures.
● Perform selected neonatal procedures safely and competently according to standard
protocols.
● Apply appropriate pain prevention and comfort measures before, during, and after
procedures.
● Identify indications, contraindications, and potential complications of common neonatal
procedures.
● Document procedures accurately, including consent, technique, and monitoring.
ROLE OF THE FACILITATOR
Facilitators play a central role in ensuring safe learning and patient protection during procedural
training. Prior to each session, facilitators should:
● Review all procedural steps and equipment requirements.
● Identify appropriate neonates or simulation alternatives.
● Coordinate with neonatal unit staff to ensure clinical safety.
● Ensure informed consent is obtained from caregivers where applicable.
● Supervise all procedures closely, intervening immediately if patient safety is compromised.
Facilitators must emphasize patient-centered care, adherence to infection prevention standards, and
reflective learning throughout all procedural demonstrations and practice sessions

GENERAL PRINCIPLES FOR NEONATAL PROCEDURES
Procedure Documentation
Facilitators must reinforce that every procedure performed on a neonate must be documented clearly,
including:
● Date and time of procedure
● Indication and diagnosis
● Consent process and caregiver discussion
● Procedure performed and technique used
● Complications (if any)
● Post-procedure monitoring and plan
Refusal of procedures and associated counseling must also be documented comprehensively
Infection Prevention and Safety
All procedures must follow universal precautions:
● Strict hand hygiene
● Use of sterile or high-level disinfected equipment
● Maintenance of a clean and organized procedural field
● Appropriate disposal of sharps and contaminated materials
These principles are reinforced during clinical practice sessions within the neonatal unit
Pain Prevention and Comfort Measures
Facilitators should ensure that participants consistently apply pain-prevention strategies, including:
Environmental and Behavioral Measures
● Swaddling during procedures
● Non-nutritive sucking
● Minimizing noise and light
● Skin-to-skin contact (Kangaroo Mother Care) following procedures
Physiological Measures
● Oral glucose/sucrose administration according to gestational age
● Gentle tactile stimulation as competitive sensory input

Complications to Name Out Loud
• Vasospasm — white or blue leg, foot or buttock. The commonest, and the earliest warning.
• Thrombosis and embolism.
• Ischaemia of the gut (NEC), kidney, or limb.
• Haemorrhage — a disconnected arterial line exsanguinates a newborn in minutes.
• Infection. Hypertension. False tract.
If a leg blanches or goes blue after a UAC: that is the catheter, until proved otherwise. Warm the
OPPOSITE leg reflexly. If it does not resolve quickly — remove the line. A line is replaceable; a
foot is not.

• Forcing at the two normal resistance points instead of waiting with steady pressure.
• Aiming cephalad, like the vein.
• Not dilating the lumen and declaring the artery ‘impossible’.
• Leaving the tip at T10–L2.
• Not looking at the legs afterwards — the whole complication set is visible on the skin.

Definition
Patient safety is defined as freedom from accidental injury. Ensuring patient safety involves the
establishment of operational systems and processes that minimise the likelihood of errors and
maximise the likelihood of intercepting them when they occur.
Then explain WHY neonatal care carries higher risk — the three reasons from your draft:
• Weight-based dosing — every dose is a fresh calculation that changes as the baby grows
• Rapid deterioration — small errors become life-threatening quickly
• Invasive procedures

the likelihood of INTERCEPTING them. That second half is the whole session. We will never stop
all errors. We can build a unit that catches them before they reach the baby.”
Importance
According to the WHO, medical errors affect 1 IN 10 PATIENTS globally, with consequences
including death, lasting or temporary harm, financial setbacks, and psychosocial distress for the
patient and sometimes the caregiver.
• The distinctive, complicated SCNU environment plus the heightened vulnerability of newborns
amplifies the likelihood of error.
Landmarks: the IOM report of 1999; the IOM 2001 report — care should be effective, evidence-
based, patient-centred, timely, efficient and equitable, and patients should not be harmed by the care
they receive.

14.1 Recognising the Baby Who Needs NIV
Why NIV, and Why It Replaced the Ventilator
Over the past few decades, invasive mechanical ventilation has been replaced by NIV, because
invasive ventilation is associated with major morbidities: bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD),
pulmonary hypertension, increased susceptibility to respiratory infection, neurodevelopmental
impairment, and cerebral palsy.
Definition: NIV refers to any method of providing respiratory support where an endotracheal tube is
NOT used.
“Every day a baby spends on a ventilator is a day their lungs are being injured to keep them alive.
NIV is how we support breathing without paying that price. The whole of this chapter is about
staying on the near side of the tube.”

Contraindications — When NIV Is the Wrong Answer
1. Severe respiratory distress, especially with cardiovascular instability — invasive ventilation may
be required.
2. Haemodynamic instability — positive pressure can affect cardiac function.
3. Severe air leak syndrome — pneumothorax or pneumomediastinum; NIV could worsen it.
4. Facial abnormalities preventing a proper seal or interface placement.
5. Unstable neurological status — may not tolerate treatment.
6. Upper airway obstruction.
7. Gastrointestinal conditions — abdominal wall anomalies or massive distension.
8. Inability to protect the airway.
9. Uncooperative neonate — extreme agitation or non-compliance.
The manual's rule: always consult the neonatal specialist / senior, and consider the individual
patient's clinical status — contraindications can vary. NIV is not for the baby who is already too sick
for it.

Advantages of NIV — Ask Before You Tell
• Preserves airway integrity; avoids invasive ventilation and its complications
• Reduces ventilator-associated pneumonia and lung injury
• Enhances parental involvement — the baby stays accessible for kangaroo care
• Improves respiratory muscle function by minimising work of breathing
• Enhances gas exchange — CPAP creates and maintains PEEP, recruits alveoli
• Decreases risk of chronic lung disease; better tolerated in preterms
• Decreases need for intubation; flexible; allows earlier weaning
Disadvantages — The Reasons This Chapter Has Six More Sessions
• Interface challenges — leak or skin breakdown
• Gastric distension → regurgitation and aspiration (why an OG tube is mandatory)

14.5 Nasal Injury: Prevent, Inspect, Stage

rows: “Nasal injury is the price of CPAP, and it is almost entirely preventable. A baby who survives
RDS and goes home with a hole in the septum was failed — not by the disease, but by the
watching. This is the session that prevents it.”
• Nasal prongs cause trauma, irritation or septal necrosis, particularly with PROLONGED use.
• The commonest mechanism is a prong bridge pressing on the columella — the strip of skin
between the nostrils — which blanches, then breaks down.

t: Prevention — Built Into Every Step Already
1. Correct prong size — biggest that fits without distending.
2. Barrier dressing (granuflex) under the nose and over the bridge.
3. The prong bridge must NOT abut the columella; must not blanch.
4. Remove prongs/mask 4-hourly to rest the nose — more often if the baby's condition dictates.
5. Loosen tapes to remove; never pull off the face.
6. Inspect and DOCUMENT at every check.

15.3 High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation (HFOV)
Teaching

rows: “Conventional ventilation gives big-ish breaths at a normal-ish rate. HFOV does the opposite —
tiny breaths, smaller than the dead space, hundreds of times a minute, on top of one constant
pressure that holds the lung open. It exists for one reason: to keep the lung open without the
damaging pressures that conventional ventilation would need.”

t: What It Is
• Rapid ventilation rates with small tidal volumes (often LESS than anatomical dead space).
• Active inspiratory AND expiratory phases.
• A constant distending airway pressure (MAP) is applied to the alveoli, maximising functional
residual capacity and V/Q matching, over which small tidal volumes are superimposed at high
rate.
Indications
1. Alternative to conventional ventilation, as a PRIMARY mode.
2. When adequate oxygenation and/or ventilation cannot be achieved on conventional ventilation
— as a RESCUE mode.
3. To minimise lung injury by avoiding high inspiratory pressures or FiO₂ on conventional
ventilation.
Disease settings where HFOV may suit: RDS · chronic lung disease of prematurity · MAS · CDH ·
air-leak syndrome with pulmonary interstitial emphysema · pneumonia · pulmonary haemorrhage ·
hypoplastic lungs.
The One Danger to Teach Hard
The disadvantage of high MAP is OVER-INFLATION of the lungs — which decreases cardiac
output, reduces BP, raises pulmonary vascular resistance, decreases venous return, and causes

FACILITATOR GUIDE Sudan Training Course on Management of Sick and Small Newborns — 2026
pulmonary leaks. It must be identified in time by clinical assessment, BP and chest X-ray, and
corrected by reducing the MAP.
“HFOV holds the lung open with one steady pressure. Too little and the lung collapses; too much
and you strangle the circulation. The chest X-ray and the blood pressure are how you tell the
difference — not the saturation alone.”
Weaning HFOV
• Primarily by reducing the MAP as compliance improves. Reduce FiO₂ as tolerated; once below
~30%, wean MAP in 1–2 cmH₂O increments (except when over-inflation is evident).
• In air-leak syndromes, reducing MAP may take priority over weaning FiO₂.
• Reduce ΔP (amplitude) in increments of 2–4 according to the PaCO₂; observe the chest wall for
vibration.
• Extubate from HFOV to CPAP, or transition to conventional ventilation first (set PEEP, then a
PIP giving a MAP 1–2 cmH₂O below the HFOV setting).

15.4 Settings: General, Then by Disease
Before You Set Anything — Define the Goal (3.6)
The manual insists the goal is chosen before the dials. Assess the pathophysiology (RDS vs MAS,
post-surfactant, lung hypoplasia), the clinical findings, the blood gas (oxygenation vs ventilation),
and the imaging. Then define ONE goal:
● Improve V/Q mismatch — but avoid oxygen toxicity, OR
● Recruit the lung — but avoid lung trauma, OR
● Support respiration — and plan for extubation as soon as indicated.
“You cannot set a ventilator without a goal, any more than you can set off on a journey without a
destination. ‘Improve the gas’ is not a goal. ‘Recruit this atelectatic lung while keeping the plateau
under 30’ is a goal.”

15.5 Caring for the Ventilated Baby

rows: “The ventilator does not care for the baby. You do. The machine delivers a breath; everything
that keeps that breath safe — the oxygen you wean, the pressure you watch, the tube you secure
— is nursing and medical work at the bedside. This session is that work.”

t: Oxygen — A Drug With a Deadline
Inspired oxygen harms the lung parenchyma after prolonged exposure through toxic oxygen radicals.
Reduce the FiO₂ to 0.5 (50%) or BELOW as soon as possible — ideally within the FIRST 24
HOURS. The primary determinants of oxygenation are FiO₂ and mean airway pressure.
“The first 24 hours has a target: FiO₂ at or below 0.5. If you are still on 0.8 at hour 20, that is not the
disease being stubborn — that is a baby who needs a plan, whether that is surfactant, recruitment, or
a mode change.”
The Pressures You Watch
• PIP reflects the pressure needed to overcome elastic recoil — the best estimate of peak alveolar
pressure, an important indicator of alveolar distension.
• Accurate peak pressure requires NO patient effort during inspiration or exhalation.
• High inspiratory pressure risks barotrauma, volutrauma, and reduced cardiac output.
Inspiratory PLATEAU pressure should ideally be < 30 cmH₂O. Elevated Pplat may be reduced by
decreasing PEEP (which may reduce oxygenation) or decreasing VT (which may reduce minute
ventilation). Permissive hypercapnia and a controlled fall in pH may be accepted when a high Pplat
must be reduced.
I:E, Auto-PEEP and the Trap of Stacking Breaths
• Total cycle time = 60 ÷ respiratory rate. Inspiration and expiration share it; normal spontaneous
I:E is ~1:2.
• In obstruction (asthma, some chronic lung disease) expiration is prolonged — I:E becomes 1:2.5

Reduce auto-PEEP by (in order of effectiveness):
● Decreasing the respiratory rate — the MOST effective way.
● Shortening the inspiratory time — extends expiration for fuller exhalation.
Decreasing VT.

rows: auto-PEEP is breath-stacking — the next breath arrives before the last one has fully left. The
instinct is to breathe FASTER to fix a rising CO₂; here that makes it worse. Slowing down is the
fix. This is counter-intuitive and worth a full minute.

t: Also Monitor
• Gas exchange, lung mechanics, work of breathing, neuromuscular capacity, metabolic status —
assessed FREQUENTLY to guide changes.
• Humidification of inspired gas.
• Remember: adjusting one parameter is likely to affect the others — take care with every change.
15.6 Ward Round — Run It Live
• 3–4 ventilated babies (or simulated stations). For each: state the mode, the settings, the last gas,
the FiO₂ trend, the Pplat, and the goal.
• Each pair decides: is this baby over-ventilated, under-ventilated, or on track — and what ONE
change (if any) they would make.
• Enforce the rule: change one thing, then reassess. Never turn three dials at once.

rows: “Weaning and extubation are two different decisions. Weaning is turning the support down.
Extubation is taking the tube out. A baby can be weaned to low settings and still not be ready to
have the tube out — and confusing the two is how babies get re-intubated.”
The manual is explicit: decisions about WEANING are separate and apart from decisions about
EXTUBATION. Some babies wean easily to low settings but are not yet ready to breathe without

t: Weaning — The Factors That Say ‘Ready to Turn It Down’
• The circumstances that required ventilation must be RESOLVING.
• Level of alertness; need for sedation.
• Respiratory drive and adequate oxygenation — SpO₂ > 95% with FiO₂ < 40% and/or low PEEP
requirement (< 7 cmH₂O).
• Adequate ventilation — PaCO₂ < 45 (no chronic respiratory failure), or > 45 with acceptable
pH.
• Time since the most recent respiratory or haemodynamic decompensation.
Permissive hypercapnia helps weaning and reduces lung injury: target PaCO₂ 50–60 while keeping
pH over 7.20 (limited by pH 7.20–7.25). Preterms on permissive hypercapnia for 10+ days showed
improved respiratory drive, fewer days on the ventilator, and a trend to less BPD or death.

15.8 Extubation steps
1. Have a written mechanical ventilation protocol — including weaning, extubation and re-
intubation criteria — agreed by neonatologists, nurses and respiratory therapists.
2. Use assist control with volume-targeted ventilation if a proximal flow sensor is available.
3. Allow permissive hypercapnia (PaCO₂ 50–60) and set SpO₂ targets (91–95%).
4. Give a LOADING DOSE OF CAFFEINE before extubation — ideally within 24 hours prior.
5. Place the infant on CPAP or NIPPV IMMEDIATELY after extubation (PEEP ≥ 5) using short
bi-nasal prongs or a nasal mask.
6. Stop enteral feeds for 4 hours before extubation.
7. Confirm acceptable weaning parameters: MAP ≤ 8 cmH₂O, FiO₂ < 30–40%, rate < 30/min with
an acceptable gas.
Step 5 is not optional. A preterm has insufficient drive and muscle strength to hold his lung open
after the tube comes out. The distending pressure goes on IMMEDIATELY — not after a wait-and-
see. Have the CPAP set up and running before you pull the tube.
Why Caffeine
• A large multi-centre RCT showed caffeine before extubation gave less BPD, shorter oxygen
duration, and intubation for almost a WEEK less.
• Early caffeine (before day 3) may further reduce time on the ventilator.
• Give within at least 24 hours of the projected extubation. (Cross-reference: caffeine prescribing
and stopping, Module 2.)
“Caffeine buys you a week off the ventilator. There are not many single drugs on this course you can
say that about. Load it before you extubate — every time.”
Post-Extubation, and When Weaning Fails
• After extubation, a distending pressure (CPAP or NIPPV) is necessary immediately to prevent
post-extubation atelectasis.
Common reasons for FAILED weaning:
• Cardiac dysfunction · cognitive dysfunction · respiratory pump failure · respiratory muscle and
diaphragmatic dysfunction · metabolic disorders

Complications of Mechanical Ventilation (3.10)
• Air leaks — pneumothorax, pulmonary interstitial emphysema (cross-reference: needle
thoracotomy and chest tube, Prematurity — RDS).
• Barotrauma and volutrauma from high pressure/volume.
• Reduced cardiac output, reduced venous return, raised pulmonary vascular resistance from high
mean airway pressure.
• Ventilator-associated pneumonia (cross-reference: sepsis prevention bundles, Module 2 Section
• Bronchopulmonary dysplasia — the chronic price the whole chapter is trying to avoid.
• Oxygen toxicity — ROP and lung injury.
Every complication above is a reason the goal was ‘support respiration and plan for extubation as
soon as indicated.’ The safest ventilator is the one the baby comes off soonest. This session and the
weaning session are the same argument from two ends.
